rows.searchedFor: can I do some paid freelance work outside my job here?
rows.answer:
The handbook says PostHog is ok with you earning money on the side, which it calls "side gigs", but not with it being your main focus and PostHog being just a paycheck.[1]

- A few hours a month on a paid side gig is acceptable, and side gigs should by default be something you work on in your personal time that does not impact the work you do at PostHog.[2]
- Side gigs, whether paid or unpaid, are fine if you are going above and beyond for PostHog and still able to look after yourself properly. The handbook says it doesn't think that's possible beyond a certain level of time/energy commitment, but it is happy for you to spend a little time on them each week.[3]
- If you want your side gig to become your full-time work one day, that is ok. Let PostHog know so it can create a plan.[4]

rows.searchedFor: Do I need to run paid freelance work outside my job by anyone first?
rows.answer:
Yes, the handbook asks you to check in with the relevant Exec team member for your team (James, Tim, or Charles) and get their confirmation before going ahead with any side gig.[1] If the side gig existed before you joined PostHog, this will usually be covered as part of the onboarding process.[2]

A few related points from the handbook:
- A few hours a month on a paid side gig is acceptable, and side gigs should by default be something you work on in your personal time without impacting your PostHog work.[3]
- If the idea started at PostHog and you want to develop it as a personal or external project, you need explicit sign-off first.[4]

rows.searchedFor: a big prospect wants a feature promised by Q3 written into their contract - is that ok?
rows.answer:
No. The handbook says PostHog doesn't contract deliverables, and especially doesn't contract to provide deliverables by a certain date, because on principle a single customer would be forcing PostHog to build something.[1] The stated reason in the enterprise principles is that otherwise a single customer could have too much of an impact on team morale and priorities.[2]

Some related points from the handbook:
- If PostHog has to walk away from a deal because it would have to compromise on these principles, it will.[3]
- PostHog will build things for a big customer as long as it is confident they won't be the only user of that thing, and re-shuffling the roadmap a bit could make sense.[4]
- Customers need to try PostHog before they expect changes, and PostHog doesn't love big requirement documents from people who haven't used the product before.[5]

rows.searchedFor: how does a YC founder get a desk at Hogpatch?
rows.answer:
A YC founder can't apply for a Hogpatch desk. Hogpatch is invite-only and isn't open to the whole batch; when space opens up, PostHog handpicks a few YC companies to join.[1] There is a waitlist, but you can't apply to it, since founders are handpicked when there's room.[2]

Once invited:
- Judy, the office manager, sends you and your cofounders a digital wallet pass that gives 24/7 self-service access.[3]
- Desks and phone booths have no booking system, so you just grab a spot when you arrive.[4]
- Each invite lasts 3 months.[5]

rows.searchedFor: why did US customers lose their older Logs data in February?
rows.answer:
A routine mutation to materialize an index finished on Feb 19 and triggered a bug in ClickHouse's zero-copy replication, which made one replica wrongly believe all of the data parts in the database were no longer referenced.[1]

- From 11:02 to 19:40, the replicas deleted all of the data stored in S3 for the entire database. Data only moves to S3 after 24 hours, and most queries are for recent data, so the volume of query errors was low and no automated alarms triggered.[2]
- PostHog lacked monitoring for the integrity of "cold" data in S3, and the deletion happened silently in the background without application-level errors, so dashboards stayed "green" until a node restart forced a consistency check.[3]
- At 19:40 a node crashed and restarted, and it failed to start because of the large volume of missing data. Engineers then found that the vast majority of S3-backed data was missing.[4]
- The result was the loss of data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region, affecting only the Logs product.[5] Kafka's 3 days of retention saved recent activity from total loss.[6]

rows.searchedFor: Did PostHog recover any of the older Logs data that US customers lost in February?
rows.answer:
The handbook says only the most recent three days of Logs data were restored, so older data was not recovered. The February 19th incident caused the loss of Logs data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region.[1] By 21:45 that day, the team had determined the data was most likely unrecoverable, and disaster recovery procedures started.[2]

- The team cut over to a new table and restored data from Kafka, which had 3 days of retention.[3]
- The backfill from Kafka history began on Feb 20 at 10:05 and completed at 12:21.[4]
- Configuring Kafka with 3 days of retention saved the team from total data loss for recent activity.[5]

rows.searchedFor: we're launching a beta soon - when do we need to start tracking which users are interested in our product?
rows.answer:
The handbook says to start tracking product intents as soon as your product is in any sort of public beta, so that data is collected for later when a good activation metric is being determined.[1] Collecting product intents should be a precursor to any sort of public release.[2]

The handbook also describes another way of gauging interest earlier:
- Adding items to the coming soon menu early lets you gauge interest in a new feature via sign-ups, and ensures betas can have sample users ready from the moment they launch.[3]
- Users who registered interest during the Concept stage can opt in once you move the item to beta.[4]

rows.searchedFor: which of my accounts are big enough to be worth visiting in person?
rows.answer:
The handbook gives two thresholds, depending on the section.

- In-person visits work best for accounts paying or likely to pay $50k+/year where you've identified specific opportunities for expansion, are navigating renewal conversations, or need to overcome significant technical or organizational hurdles.[1]
- The retention and expansion guidance says you should be trying to regularly see customers in your book of business who are $100k+ annually, or could get there.[2]
- It also says to match the cadence of in-person meetings to contract size: more regular for Very Large, less regular for Large.[3]

The handbook also calls visits a high-effort, high-reward play - use them strategically.[1] Your intuition and experience should ultimately guide the who, what and how of in-person meetings.[4]

rows.searchedFor: how do I pull the posthog org IDs for all my accounts out of salesforce?
rows.answer:
You can get your organization IDs with a SQL query: SELECT DISTINCT posthog_org_id_c, NULL as empty_column FROM salesforce.account WHERE owner_id = 'your_salesforce_id', then export the results via CSV.[1]

- This works by querying PostHog's data warehouse to pull Salesforce data and create a CSV of all PostHog organization IDs for accounts you own, which gives you the list of orgs to monitor.[2]
- To find your Salesforce ID, go to your profile and copy the text in the website URL after "/User/".[1]
- The empty column is there so the org IDs are comma-delimited, which lets you copy and paste them directly into a filter input text field.[1]

rows.searchedFor: how can I see what posthog is doing on a customer's live site?
rows.answer:
You can append ?__posthog_debug=true to a site that has PostHog running, which can show lots of useful information like logs and config.[1]

- If the customer isn't using session replay, add ?__posthog_debug=true to a URL where PostHog is being called, pull up the console logs, type posthog.config, and look for the api_host property.[2]
- If the customer is using session replay, go to the relevant replay video, select Activity > Inspector > Doctor, and search for "config". Look for PostHog Config and expand api_host to see whether the URL is one of PostHog's domains or one of the customer's own.[3]
- If neither method is available because the customer isn't using session replay and the hosted site isn't publicly accessible, you can ask the customer on the discovery call.[4]

rows.searchedFor: How can I check if a customer has set up a reverse proxy for PostHog tracking on their live site?
rows.answer:
If the customer isn't using session replay, you can add ?__posthog_debug=true to a URL where PostHog is being called, pull up the console logs, type posthog.config and look for the api_host property.[1] If api_host shows us.i.posthog or eu.i.posthog, they are not using a reverse proxy.[2]

Other options:
- If the customer is using session replay, open the replay video, select Activity > Inspector > Doctor, search for "config", find PostHog Config, and expand api_host to see whether the URL is one of PostHog's domains (us.i.posthog.com or eu.i.posthog.com) or one of the customer's own.[3]
- If neither method is available because the customer isn't using session replay and the hosted site isn't publicly accessible, you can ask the customer on the discovery call.[4]
- With either PostHog's managed reverse proxy or a non-managed one, events should populate the "Library custom API host" property. Host mapping and domains can potentially be seen in Metabase, and you should verify the setup with the customer.[5]

rows.answer:
- On-call involves weekends too (unlike Support Hero), because the stability of production systems is critical.[1]
- The global on-call schedule has 2 weekend layers: Europe Weekend (06:00 to 18:00 UTC, 12 hours) and Americas Weekend (18:00 to 06:00 UTC, 12 hours).[2]
- If you can't cover a shift, you can request cover and trade whole weeks or just specific days.[3]
